content.p: For more than three years, the question in southeastern Michigan was whether Dee Warner had walked away from her life or been taken from it. Her adult children reported her missing on 25 April 2021 after they could not find her at the home she shared with her husband, Dale, in Lenawee County, about 70 miles southwest of Detroit. In August 2024 investigators found her remains wrapped in tarps and sealed inside a welded fertilizer tank in a barn on land that Dale Warner owned.

On 10 March 2026 a Lenawee County jury found Warner, 58, guilty of second-degree murder and of tampering with evidence. On 7 May 2026 Judge Michael R. Olsaver sentenced him to a combined minimum of more than 32 years and a maximum of 70. Warner had pleaded not guilty and did not testify. His lawyer said he maintains his innocence and that she expects an appeal.

Dee Ann Warner was 52 when she vanished. She and Dale had married in 2006, the Detroit News reported, and NBC News reported that she had five children and ran both a trucking company and a farming business. The Warners owned several enterprises, among them a farm, a company supplying equipment to other farms and a trucking firm, according to the prosecutor's opening statement as reported by FOX 2.

Witnesses at trial described a marriage that had become a business partnership and then a battleground. By 2021, according to testimony reported by the Detroit News, both the marriage and the businesses were struggling, and the couple bickered over children, money and the farm and trucking operations. Prosecutors told jurors that Dale suspected his wife of having an affair and spied on her. A General Motors data analyst testified that a phone app had been used to check the location of Dee's Cadillac Escalade 2,100 times between January 2020 and April 2021. Witnesses also said he had a worker clone her phone, and that in 2020 another employee bought a GPS tracker for her Hummer. Police told the court they found notes in which he recorded her activities, opinions and text conversations.

Dale told police the couple's arguments were loud but never physical. Other witnesses disagreed. Dee's massage therapist, Stacey Brodie, testified that she saw bruises on Dee's body eight to 10 times, including one on her hip that looked like a handprint.

Prosecutors said the final break came on Saturday 24 April 2021. According to FOX 2's account of the opening statements, Dee was upset after Dale allegedly told farmworkers that she took Xanax and was "a mess". She told him, prosecutors said, that the marriage was over and that the businesses would be sold. One of her daughters testified that Dee came into the house hysterically crying and said she was done.

Dale gave police a different account. As summarised by the prosecutor, he said Dee was upset that night but calmed down and fell asleep on the living-room couch, and that when he woke on Sunday to work on the farm he last saw her there. He told investigators he believed she had left of her own accord, and suggested she might have become addicted to oxycodone prescribed for neck pain. At trial Dr. Cho testified that toxicology found no evidence of oxycodone.

Dee's children, who had an open invitation to Sunday breakfast, arrived to find her gone. They searched, then reported her missing on 25 April. They said it was unusual, because she almost always answered texts and calls right away. FOX 2 reported that, according to the prosecutor, the children called police privately because Dale allegedly did not want officers involved.

The Lenawee County Sheriff's Office led the case at first. Detective Kevin Greca walked the farm on 27 April 2021 with Dale's permission, and body-camera video later played in court showed him checking vehicles and barns. Greca testified that the farm's tanks did not concern him: "A farm is expected to have tanks." The Michigan State Police took over in August 2022 at the sheriff's request, after a task force of state police and FBI personnel was formed in March 2022 to assist. 13abc counted three pushes behind the November 2023 charge against Dale Warner: a public campaign, a 4,000-acre property search and the effort to have her declared legally dead. The campaign was called "Justice for Dee" and was led by her brother, Gregg Hardy.

The family also asked a court to declare Dee legally dead. WXYZ reported that she was legally declared dead in March 2024. FOX 2 said a declaration-of-death trial had to be held before Dale could be charged without a body. CBS Detroit, in a separate report, said the family had filed the petition in 2022.

State police told NBC News on 22 November 2023 that investigators had "pieced together a very difficult case" with "unique challenges" because no body had been found. Dale Warner, then 55, was arrested at home and arraigned the next day on one count of open murder and one of tampering with evidence. CBS Detroit reported that officers who reviewed Dee's personal and financial records in 2023 found activity that stopped suddenly, and that a query run on her in the state's police database never showed her found. Officials said this led them to believe she had not left voluntarily. Warner was arraigned in June 2024 and bound over for trial.

According to testimony, state police detectives developed what they called a "welding theory": that Dee's body had been put inside one of the many fertilizer tanks stored on Warner property. Retired detective Scott Singleton said investigators had evidence of internet searches about burying anhydrous tanks. In August 2024 Daniel Drewyor, now a state police detective lieutenant, decided to look at all the tanks stored on Warner properties.

On 16 August 2024, Drewyor testified, officers searched properties on Paragon and Carson highways. One tank stood by itself in a barn on the Paragon property. It was painted white, had a weld on one end that had not come from the factory, and bore a hand-written tag reading "Out of Service Bad Dip tube" on one side and "Do Not Fill" on the other. Police towed it to the Ambassador Bridge in Detroit to be X-rayed. The image showed what appeared to be a body. Michigan State Police announced on Sunday 18 August that remains had been found during the execution of a search warrant on Warner's property. They were identified three days later through dental records, and the Jackson County Medical Examiner's Office ruled her death a homicide.

Dr. Patrick Cho, who performed the autopsy on 20 August, testified that the body was wrapped in two polyethylene tarps secured with duct tape. The legs were bound, the arms were bound to the torso, and tape covered the nose, mouth and part of the head. He found blunt-force injuries to the head, subdural hemorrhages, bruising at the back of the tongue and pinpoint hemorrhages in the epiglottis. He gave the causes of death as strangulation and blunt-force trauma, either of which could have killed her, and the manner as homicide. The condition of the body alone could not have established when she died; the date of on or about 25 April 2021 rested on when law enforcement said she was last known to be alive.

Testimony began on 12 February 2026. The prosecution's case, as the Tecumseh Herald summarised it, was that Warner killed Dee by strangulation and blunt-force trauma on the night of 24 to 25 April 2021 at their home on Munger Road in Franklin Township. It alleged he then bound her body, wrapped it in tarps, cut open an old anhydrous ammonia tank, put her inside, welded it shut and eventually moved it to the Paragon Road property. Fox News quoted Wyse as telling jurors that Warner could have called 911 and said, "I screwed up".
The evidence was largely circumstantial, the Detroit News reported. Among what jurors were shown or told:

Farm security video showed Warner on 25 April 2021 holding an angle grinder, a length of chain and welding equipment. Singleton testified that the footage let him build a timeline of when Warner might have been in the farm's spray barn. At 6:37 p.m. a front-end loader left the area with something white in its bucket, and two minutes later the round end of a white tank appeared among items in the burn pile where it had not been before. Welding inspector Justin Schmidt, who examined the tank, said the repair weld was not liquid-tight, because white paint had leaked through it, and that he estimated 50 minutes or more to cut the tank and between 21.3 and 35.5 minutes to weld it, work one person could do. A state police forensic scientist, Amanda Isett, told the jury that Warner's left middle fingerprint was on the adhesive side of one of the "ammonia" stickers on the tank.

Witnesses testified that drone images showed Warner using a loader to move a rusted fertilizer tank from the burn pile after he learned police planned to use cadaver dogs. A state police dog handler testified that ammonia fumes would probably mask odours a dog would otherwise detect, and that a sealed tank would stop the scent escaping. Electronic devices contained searches for "chemical cremation", police said.

The defence told jurors the case rested on "speculation, assumption and innuendo". Chartier argued that farm cameras tracked Warner's movements all day and left too little time for the sequence prosecutors described. She also noted that searches had never found blood or signs of a struggle in the home. The defence called Warner's ex-wife, an employee of the trucking company and Gregg Hardy as witnesses before resting on 3 March.

Jury deliberations began on Thursday 5 March. They stopped when a juror had an emergency, and resumed on Tuesday 10 March. The verdict, read at 5:20 p.m., was second-degree murder and tampering with evidence. Jurors had also been able to convict on first-degree murder; the Detroit News reported the jury chose second degree. Hardy said he was disappointed the jury did not reach first-degree murder but exuberant for his sister.

At sentencing on 7 May, Dee's sister-in-law Shelley Hardy removed the yellow "Justice for Dee" bracelet she had worn since Dee went missing. Judge Olsaver imposed 31 years and three months to 60 years for murder and 17 months to 10 years for tampering, and ordered them served consecutively, although sentences for multiple charges normally run concurrently. Warner received credit for 898 days served on the murder count. The judge said this was not a case of shredded documents or flushed drugs: "Mr. Warner welded his wife's deceased body into a fertilizer tank where it remained for more than three years." Her family, he said, was deprived of the chance to grieve while they searched for her.

Dee's children spoke in court. Rikkel Bock said Warner had cut off contact between her youngest sister and the rest of the family and had made the child believe their mother had walked out. Warner declined to comment.

On 3 March 2025 state police announced that Dale's son Jaron Warner, 28, faced charges of tampering with evidence and of being an accessory after a felony. The prosecutor's office dismissed the case on 13 May 2025, saying it could not locate a witness and that charges could be refiled if that person were found. His lawyers said he committed no crime. 13abc's coverage list also records a civil lawsuit against Dale Warner seeking $100 million for Dee's children.
Warner's lawyer said she expects an appeal. No appeal result has been reported.
